result.markdown: --- title: "Sensitivity and identifiability" course-unit: ch14-sensitivity-and-identifiability status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - **Sensitivity:** which inputs move a chosen output? - **Identifiability:** which parameters can the observation process distinguish? - A narrow optimizer interval is not evidence that every biological parameter is learned. ::: {.notes} Three minutes, and set the shape of the session: three tools, one question each. Local sensitivity asks what happens if I nudge a parameter. Global sensitivity asks which parameter is responsible for the spread in outcomes across a whole plausible range. Structural identifiability asks a different kind of question altogether: not what the model does, but what the data could ever tell us about it. Keep one distinction visible all session, because everything here turns on it: perturbing a model is not the same as learning from data. This is also the last slot of a long day, so promise the payoff early. The session ends by proving something about this afternoon's reporting fraction. ::: ## Baseline SIR model Deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model: $$ \dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad \dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad \dot R=\gamma I. $$ At the course baseline, $N=1000$, $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$, $(\beta,c,\gamma)=(0.05,10,0.25)$, and $\mathcal R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$. The state sensitivity matrix is $J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial(\beta,c,\gamma)$. ::: {.notes} Two minutes. Same baseline as every other session, so nothing here is new except the notation for the sensitivity matrix. Plant one seed and move on: beta and c never appear apart in these equations, only as the product beta-c. Ask the room what that might mean for estimating them separately, take one answer, and say the last part of the session settles it. One warning about the parameterisation: from here the code uses a positional vector [beta, c, gamma] rather than the named tuple of the earlier sessions, because the sensitivity and Sobol APIs index parameters by position. The worksheet flags this too. ::: ## Before any theory: sweep and look {.smaller} Choose parameter sets, run the model for each, look at what comes out. It commits to nothing about the model's structure, and it is the most expensive method in the session. A grid scales badly: three parameters at ten levels is a thousand runs, and most differ from a neighbour in one coordinate only. A **Latin hypercube** divides each range into $n$ strata and samples each once, so every one-dimensional projection gets $n$ distinct values instead of $n^{1/3}$. ::: {#cell-slide-ch14-design .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using QuasiMonteCarlo, OrdinaryDiffEq, StableRNGs, Statistics lower = [0.02, 5.0, 0.15] # β, c, γ upper = [0.08, 15.0, 0.40] design = QuasiMonteCarlo.sample(200, lower, upper, LatinHypercubeSample(StableRNG(20250916))) size(design) ``` ::: {#slide-ch14-design .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, 200) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The seed is not decoration. An unseeded design changes every number on this slide at every render, and the same is true of the worksheet. Make the stratification concrete: with 200 samples and a grid you would get about six distinct values per parameter; with a Latin hypercube you get 200. Since you usually do not know in advance which parameter matters, spreading the budget across every one-dimensional projection is the safer bet. ::: ## One model, two hundred parameter sets {.smaller} ::: {#cell-slide-ch14-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sweep_sir!(du, u, p, t) β, c, γ = p incidence = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / 1000.0 du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * u[2] du[3] = γ * u[2] end sweep_grid = collect(0.0:0.25:40.0) base_problem = ODEProblem(sweep_sir!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), [0.05, 10.0, 0.25]) sweep = solve( EnsembleProblem(base_problem; prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> remake(prob, p = design[:, ctx.sim_id])), Tsit5(); trajectories = 200, saveat = sweep_grid, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9) length(sweep.u) ``` ::: {#slide-ch14-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 200 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} `prob_func` is the same hook as yesterday's jump ensembles; only what it varies has changed. There it gave each trajectory a new seed, which is replication; here it gives each trajectory a column of the design, which is a sweep. Same machinery, and worth saying explicitly, because people file "run it many times" and "vary the parameters" as different problems. Two API details that waste people's time. The signature is `(prob, ctx)` with `ctx.sim_id`, not the `(prob, i, repeat)` you will find in older material. And the trajectories are `sweep.u`; iterating the solution itself flattens it. ::: ## What the sweep already knows {.smaller} ::: {#cell-slide-ch14-correlations .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} peaks = [maximum(trajectory[2, :]) for trajectory in sweep.u] β_s, c_s, γ_s = design[1, :], design[2, :], design[3, :] (β = round(cor(peaks, β_s); digits = 3), c = round(cor(peaks, c_s); digits = 3), βc = round(cor(peaks, β_s .* c_s); digits = 3), γ = round(cor(peaks, γ_s); digits = 3), R₀ = round(cor(peaks, β_s .* c_s ./ γ_s); digits = 3)) ``` ::: {#slide-ch14-correlations .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (β = 0.623, c = 0.566, βc = 0.835, γ = -0.401, R₀ = 0.988) ``` ::: ::: Neither $\beta$ nor $c$ predicts the peak on its own. Their **product** does better than either, and $R_0$ predicts it almost exactly. ::: {.notes} Stop on this slide. With no algebra at all, two hundred model runs have found the result the rest of the session proves: the model does not depend on beta and c separately, only on their product. That is the confounding the structural identifiability analysis will confirm at the end. It is worth being honest that correlation is a crude summary — it would miss a non-monotone dependence entirely, which is exactly why Sobol indices exist. But as a first look it has cost nothing but compute and has already told you where to aim. ::: ## Two hundred runs, one picture {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch14-sweep .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch14-sweep .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Two hundred Latin hypercube parameter sets: trajectories coloured by R₀, and peak prevalence against β alone and against the product βc. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Let them look before you speak. On the left, the colouring does the work: the trajectories sort almost perfectly by R nought, so one derived number explains nearly all the variation among two hundred runs. On the right is the same point as a scatter. Against beta alone the cloud is wide and shapeless; against the product it collapses onto a curve. Both axes are scaled to their own maximum so the two can share one panel — the shape is the message, not the position. ::: ## Local sensitivity: a derivative, not an uncertainty interval {.center .smaller} For a small perturbation, $$ \Delta z\approx\nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta. $$ Raw derivatives carry the units of their own parameter: since the model uses only $k=\beta c$, $\partial I/\partial\beta=c\,\partial I/\partial k$ and $\partial I/\partial c=\beta\,\partial I/\partial k$, a factor $c/\beta=200$ apart wherever they are nonzero. The elasticity $(\theta_j/I)\,\partial I/\partial\theta_j$ is dimensionless and comparable across parameters. ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch10-local .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch10-local .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Centered local derivatives of infectious prevalence, raw and as dimensionless elasticities. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Eight minutes, and the curves are worth reading aloud rather than summarising. Each one is the derivative of infectious prevalence with respect to one parameter, over time. They start at zero, since at day zero nothing has happened yet, peak around the epidemic peak, and change sign afterwards, because raising transmission moves the epidemic *earlier* as well as higher, so late in the window a bigger beta means fewer people still infectious. Read the left panel first and let the room fall into the trap. Beta looks overwhelming and c looks like a flat line at zero. Ask whether that means beta matters more, then spring it: the two curves differ by exactly two hundred, which is c over beta. Beta is measured per contact and c in contacts per day, so the derivatives are in different units and the comparison is meaningless. Nudging beta by 0.01 is a twenty percent change; nudging c by 0.01 is nothing at all. The right panel divides that out, asking instead for the percentage change in I per percentage change in each parameter. Now beta and c lie exactly on top of each other, which is why c is dashed — otherwise it would be invisible. That coincidence is the session in one picture: nothing in this plot could tell the two apart, and Worksheet Part A has them verify it numerically. Two warnings. This is a derivative at one parameter vector, so it says nothing about behaviour a long way from the baseline; that is the next slide. And a derivative is not an uncertainty interval and not a posterior; a large derivative means a parameter matters, not that we know it badly. ::: ## Where the derivatives come from {.smaller} The augmented system solves the model and its Jacobian together. Differentiating $\dot x = f(x,\theta)$ with respect to $\theta$ gives the **variational equations** $$ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}, $$ solved alongside the states rather than by re-running the model. - **Forward** (`ODEForwardSensitivityProblem`): cost grows with the number of *parameters*. Good here — three of them. - **Adjoint**: cost grows with the number of *outputs*. Use it when fitting a neural component or a model with hundreds of parameters. ::: {.notes} Six minutes. The distinction is worth drawing on the board as two rectangles: forward solves one extra trajectory per parameter, adjoint solves one extra backwards pass per output. With three parameters and a whole trajectory as output, forward wins easily; invert those numbers and it reverses. Stress that this is not a finite difference. There is no perturbation size to choose and no cancellation to worry about, which is exactly why the agreement check later matters: it confirms the finite difference we plotted was fine, not that the library was. ::: ## A derivative is not an uncertainty Three things the left-hand panel cannot tell you: - **Not an interval.** A large $\partial I/\partial\beta$ says $I$ moves when $\beta$ moves — not that $\beta$ is poorly known. - **Not global.** It holds near $\theta_0$. The sign of every curve flips after the peak, because raising transmission moves the epidemic *earlier* as well as higher. - **Not identifiability.** $\beta$ and $c$ have perfectly good, large derivatives, and are still impossible to separate. ::: {.notes} Four minutes, and it is the slide people misremember most often. Say the third bullet twice: sensitivity and identifiability are routinely conflated, and the rest of the session is built on keeping them apart. A parameter can be highly influential and completely unidentifiable at the same time — beta and c are the proof, sitting right there in the previous figure. The sign flip is worth pausing on too, because it looks like a bug the first time you see it. Late in the window a larger beta means fewer people still infectious, since the epidemic has already burned through. ::: ## Global variation: sharing out the variance {.center .smaller} Vary all three parameters across a plausible box and ask how much of the *variance* in peak prevalence each one accounts for: - $S_1$: the share that parameter explains **on its own**. - $S_T$: its share **including every interaction** it takes part in. $S_T > S_1$ means the parameter matters in combination with others; $\sum_i S_1^i < 1$ is the part of the variance no single parameter owns. ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch10-global .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch10-global .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One-at-a-time swings and Sobol indices over the same parameter box. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Ten minutes, and it is the heart of the session. Walk the left panel first: move one parameter from the bottom of its range to the top, holding the others at baseline, and record the swing. It gives a ranking, and it is what most people do by hand. Then say what it cannot see: it never leaves the baseline for the other two parameters, so a parameter that only matters when transmission is already high looks unimportant. The right panel varies all three together. Point at the gap between the blue and orange bars: that gap is interaction. Here the first-order shares sum to roughly 0.85 — nearer 0.89 on a far larger design — so of the order of a tenth of the variance belongs to no parameter individually. Both panels depend entirely on the box; widen the bounds and the ranking can change, which is the caveat to state out loud. One caveat that the next slide will sharpen. Beta and c get separate bars here only because we sampled them as two independent uniforms, and the sizes of those bars follow from the two boxes we chose, not from anything the model distinguishes. Sobol answers which input ranges drive the spread in the output; it never answers which parameters could be estimated. Anyone reading a taller beta bar as "we can measure beta" has confused the two questions, which is exactly what the observation map settles next. Two footnotes if asked. The package warns that its design matrices are not fully independent QMC sequences; that is suppressed here for legibility and does not change the picture at this sample size. And 500 samples is deliberate: the worksheet repeats this at 32 and shows the indices are unstable, even negative, when the sample is too small. ::: ## The design is part of the answer {.smaller} Sobol indices are estimates, and small designs lie: | samples | $S_1$ for $c$ | |---|---| | 32 | ≈ 0.19 | | 16384 | ≈ 0.26 | Two further choices that silently enter every sample: - **The box.** Widen the bounds and the ranking can change. The indices are conditional on ranges you chose. - **The output definition.** The peak is read from dense output on a sub-daily grid: the daily grid gives $158.09$ at day 18, the continuous peak $158.45$ near $t=17.5$. A discretisation artefact would enter every evaluation. ::: {.notes} Seven minutes. The table is the part to dwell on, because it is a live trap. At 32 samples the indices are not merely imprecise, they can come out negative, which is impossible for a variance share and is the clearest possible sign the design is too small. The worksheet has them reproduce that. The output-definition point sounds pedantic until you notice it applies to every sample in the design, not just the baseline. A quarter of a person is nothing; a systematic quarter of a person, sampled the same wrong way thousands of times, becomes a bias in the variance attribution rather than noise that averages out. ::: ## What Sobol assumes {.smaller} $$ \operatorname{Var}(z)=\sum_i V_i+\sum_{i :nonidentifiable c => :nonidentifiable g => :globally b*c => :globally ``` ::: ::: `b` and `c` come back **nonidentifiable**; `b*c` and `g` are **globally identifiable**. ::: {.notes} Eight minutes. The key conceptual move is that this model object is not the `sir10!` function we have been solving. `@parameters` makes symbols, not numbers, and the tilde records a relationship rather than assigning a value. Because it stays symbolic, the package reasons about every trajectory at once, not about one numerical solution. `funcs_to_check` is what makes the result useful rather than merely discouraging. Asking only about `b` and `c` returns two "nonidentifiable" verdicts and nothing actionable; asking additionally about the product tells you precisely what the data *can* pin down. That is the quantity to report, and the quantity to put a prior on. If it is slow to appear, say why: this compiles for tens of seconds on a cold session, which is why it is rendered here rather than typed live. ::: ## What background knowledge can and cannot buy {.smaller} Two confoundings that look alike and behave differently: | | Observed | Fixed by knowing the initial state? | |---|---|---| | $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,\,c/a)$ | $y=\beta cSI/N$ | **No** | | $(\rho,\beta c)$ | $y=\rho C(t)$ | **Yes** | The reporting fraction is rescued because declaring $S(0),I(0),R(0),C(0)$ breaks the scaling symmetry. The $\beta$–$c$ confounding is not, because $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves **every trajectory** unchanged — there is nothing left for an initial condition to pin down. Without `known_ic`, `assess_identifiability` treats initial conditions as generic unknowns, which is the stricter question. ::: {.notes} Seven minutes, and the contrast is the most useful thing in the session for anyone who fits models. Both are "two parameters we cannot separate", and the fixes are completely different: one needs an assumption you already hold, the other needs new measurement — contact data, or a c measured independently. Be precise about the wording: "the initial state", not "the population size". The worksheet marks all four initial values known, which is a stronger assumption than knowing N alone, and the distinction matters if anyone tries to reproduce it. No optimiser repairs the second row. If the information is absent from the observation map, a confident-looking estimate is an artefact of the prior or of the stopping rule. ::: ## Three questions, three tools {.smaller} | Question | Tool | Depends on | |---|---|---| | How does the output move *here*? | local sensitivity | one $\theta_0$ | | What drives the *spread* over a range? | Sobol indices | the box, the design | | What can the data *distinguish at all*? | structural identifiability | the observation map | $\beta$ and $c$ run through all three: a 200-fold spurious gap in raw derivatives, two separate Sobol bars, and provably inseparable. Only the third question is about the data. ::: {.notes} Five minutes. Draw the thread explicitly, because it is the spine of the session and the thing worth remembering a year later. The same pair of parameters looked dramatically different, then merely different, then identical — and only the last verdict is a fact about what the data contain. The first two were facts about units and about sampling choices we made. Ask the room which of the three they have seen reported in a paper without the third. It is usually all of them. ::: ## API and validation {.smaller} The derivatives above came from finite differences. The library computes them directly, by solving the variational equations alongside the model: ::: {#cell-ch10-forward-sensitivity .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#ch10-forward-sensitivity .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (saved_times = 41, relative_difference = 7.0e-5) ``` ::: ::: - `SciMLSensitivity`: forward sensitivities or adjoints. - `GlobalSensitivity`: Sobol first-order and total indices. - `StructuralIdentifiability`: `assess_identifiability`, run in the worksheet. - Validate: check $S+I+R=N$, and one derivative two ways, as above. ::: {.notes} Five minutes. The point of running this live is that the augmented problem and the finite differences agree to about one part in ten thousand, so the earlier plot was not an artefact of the perturbation size, and you now have the API that scales to models where finite differences would be hopeless. Worth one aside if the room is with you: that agreement needs tight solver tolerances on both slides. A centered difference subtracts two trajectories that differ in the fifth decimal place, so at the default tolerances the same comparison only agrees to a couple of percent, and the error is in the finite difference, not in the library. That is the practical argument for the variational equations even when a finite difference is available. The one API not executed here is `assess_identifiability`: it compiles for tens of seconds on a cold session, which is not something to do in front of an audience. That is why it lives in the worksheet, and why the warm-up cell during the break matters. Say that out loud rather than skipping past it. ::: ## Takeaways and limitations {.smaller} - Local: neighborhood behavior around one parameter vector. - Global: ranking conditional on ranges and a design. - Structural: information available in an idealized observation map, and in what you already know, such as the initial state. - Practical identifiability also depends on noise, sampling, initial states, and misspecification. Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/14-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html) for derivations and exercises; see the [SciMLSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/), [GlobalSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/), and [StructuralIdentifiability](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/) documentation for APIs. ::: {.notes} Four minutes, and it is the last thing anyone hears on Day 2, so land it rather than reading the bullets. Ask which of the session's conclusions are about the model and which are about the data. The Sobol ranking is about the model and the box we chose; the identifiability results are about the data and what we already know. Confusing the two is how people end up reporting a confident estimate of a quantity their data never contained. Then hand over to tomorrow: sensitivity tells you which parameter to spend effort on, and the intervention session asks what to do about it. Flag that Part C of the worksheet is where the reporting-fraction result gets proved, and that the two inference chapters it points at are self-study, not sessions here. :::
